Explain in your own words what 'Background to the Emergency' refers to.
questions.a: The period before the Emergency was marked by economic difficulties, rising popular movements, and a confrontation between the government and the judiciary, creating conditions that culminated in the declaration of the Emergency in 1975.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Background to the Emergency'.
questions.a: Economic crisis, popular unrest, and judicial-government conflict weakened the democratic order and set the stage for the Emergency.

Explain in your own words what 'Declaration of Emergency' refers to.
questions.a: On the advice of the Prime Minister, the President declared a state of internal emergency under Article 352 on 25 June 1975, citing internal disturbance as the ground.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Declaration of Emergency'.
questions.a: The Emergency was declared using the constitutional provision of 'internal disturbance', a controversial ground that was later removed by the 44th Amendment.

Explain in your own words what 'Emergency Provisions in the Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The Constitution provides for three types of Emergency: national Emergency (Article 352), state Emergency or President's Rule (Article 356), and financial Emergency (Article 360), each with distinct grounds and effects.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Emergency Provisions in the Constitution'.
questions.a: Emergency provisions allow the central government to assume extraordinary powers, but they must be used cautiously to preserve democratic principles.

questions.a: During the Emergency, fundamental rights of citizens were suspended, including the right to move courts for enforcement of rights under Article 32, leading to widespread arrests and curbs on freedom of speech and press.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Suspension of Fundamental Rights'.
questions.a: Suspension of fundamental rights during the Emergency raised serious questions about the balance between state power and citizen liberties.

Explain in your own words what 'Shah Commission of Inquiry' refers to.
questions.a: The Shah Commission was appointed by the Janata government in 1977 to inquire into the excesses committed during the Emergency, documenting abuse of power and violations of democratic norms.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Shah Commission of Inquiry'.
questions.a: The Shah Commission's findings revealed the extent of misuse of Emergency powers and underscored the need for constitutional safeguards.

questions.a: The Emergency taught that democratic freedoms and constitutional safeguards cannot be taken for granted, and that internal emergency provisions can be misused, requiring legal and institutional protections.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Lessons of the Emergency'.
questions.a: The Emergency remains a reminder of the fragility of democracy and the importance of vigilant institutions and citizen awareness.

Explain in your own words what 'Politics after the Emergency' refers to.
questions.a: After the Emergency, the Janata Party came to power in 1977, but internal divisions and instability led to its collapse, and the Congress returned to power in 1980, shaping the trajectory of Indian politics.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Politics after the Emergency'.
questions.a: The post-Emergency period saw the rise and fall of the Janata experiment and the return of the Congress, illustrating the resilience and complexity of Indian democracy.
